{{Short description|Branch of algebraic geometry}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Schubert calculus'''<ref name="KL">{{cite journal | last1=Kleiman | first1=S.L.| last2=Laksov | first2=Dan |author1-link=Steven Kleiman |author2-link=Dan Laksov|title= Schubert Calculus | publisher=American Mathematical Society|journal = American Mathematical Monthly | volume=79| issue=10 | year=1972 | issn=0377-9017 | doi=10.1080/00029890.1972.11993188 | pages=1061–1082 }}</ref> is a branch of [[algebraic geometry]] introduced in the nineteenth century by [[Hermann Schubert]] in order to solve various counting problems of [[projective geometry]] and, as such, is viewed as part of [[enumerative geometry]]. Giving it a more rigorous foundation was the aim of [[Hilbert's problems | Hilbert's 15th problem]].  It is related to several more modern concepts, such as  [[characteristic class]]es, and both its algorithmic aspects and applications remain of current interest. The term '''Schubert calculus''' is sometimes used to mean the enumerative geometry of linear subspaces of a vector space, which is roughly equivalent to describing the cohomology ring of Grassmannians. Sometimes it is used to mean the more general enumerative geometry of algebraic varieties that are homogenous spaces of simple Lie groups. Even more generally, '''Schubert calculus''' is sometimes understood as encompassing the study of analogous questions in [[generalized cohomology theories]].

The objects introduced by Schubert are the '''Schubert cells''',<ref name="Fu">{{cite book | last=Fulton | first= William |author-link=William Fulton (mathematician)| title= Young Tableaux. With Applications to Representation Theory and Geometry, Chapt. 9.4 | year=1997 | series =London Mathematical Society Student Texts | volume = 35 |publisher=Cambridge University Press | location = Cambridge, U.K.| isbn= 9780521567244 | doi=10.1017/CBO9780511626241 }} </ref> which are [[locally closed]] sets in a [[Grassmannian]] defined by conditions of [[incidence (geometry)|incidence]] of a [[linear subspace]] in projective space with a given [[Flag (linear algebra)|flag]]. For further details see [[Schubert variety]].

The [[intersection theory]]<ref name = "Fu1">{{cite book | last1=Fulton | first1=William | author1-link=William Fulton (mathematician) | title=Intersection Theory | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | location=Berlin, New York | isbn=978-0-387-98549-7 | mr=1644323 | year=1998 }}</ref> of these cells, which can be seen as the product structure in the [[cohomology ring]] of the Grassmannian, consisting of associated [[cohomology class]]es, allows
in particular the determination of cases in which the intersections of cells results in a [[finite set]] of points. A key result is that the Schubert cells (or rather, the classes of their Zariski closures, the '''Schubert cycles''' or '''[[Schubert varieties]]''') span the whole cohomology ring.

The combinatorial aspects mainly arise in relation to computing intersections of Schubert cycles. Lifted from the [[Grassmannian]], which is a [[homogeneous space]], to the [[general linear group]] that acts on it, similar questions are involved in the [[Bruhat decomposition]] and classification of [[Borel subgroup|parabolic subgroups]] (as [[block matrix|block triangular]] matrices).

== Construction ==
Schubert calculus can be constructed using the [[Chow ring]]
<ref name = "Fu1"/> of the [[Grassmannian]], where the generating cycles are represented by geometrically defined data.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|url=https://scholar.harvard.edu/files/joeharris/files/000-final-3264.pdf|title=3264 and All That|pages=132, section 4.1; 200, section 6.2.1}}</ref> Denote the Grassmannian of <math>k</math>-planes in a fixed <math>n</math>-dimensional vector space <math>V</math> over a field <math>F</math> as <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k,V)</math>, and its Chow ring as <math>A^*(\mathbf{Gr}(k,V))</math>. (Note that the Grassmannian is sometimes denoted <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k,n)</math> if the vector space is not explicitly given or as <math>\mathbb{G}(k-1,n-1)</math> if the ambient space <math>V</math> and its <math>k</math>-dimensional subspaces are replaced by their projectivizations.) Choosing an (arbitrary) [[flag manifold | complete flag]] over <math>F</math>
::<math>\mathcal{V} = (V_1 \subset \cdots \subset V_{n-1} \subset V_n = V), \quad \dim{V}_i = i, \quad i=1 , \dots , n, </math>

to each weakly decreasing <math>k</math>-tuple of integers <math>\mathbf{a} = (a_1,\ldots, a_k)</math>, where
::<math>n-k \geq a_1 \geq a_2 \geq \cdots \geq a_k \geq 0,</math>

i.e., to each [[Partition (number theory) |partition]] of weight
:: <math>\mathopen|\mathbf{a}\mathclose| = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i, </math>

whose [[Young diagram]] fits into the <math>k \times (n-k)</math> rectangular one for the partition <math>(n-k)^k</math>, we associate a '''Schubert variety'''<ref name="KL"/><ref name="Fu"/> (or '''Schubert cycle''') <math>\Sigma_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathcal{V}) \subset \mathbf{Gr}(k,V)</math>, defined as
::<math>\Sigma_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathcal{V}) = \{ w \in \mathbf{Gr}(k,V)(F) : \dim (V_{n-k +i - a_i} \cap w) \geq i \text{ for } i = 1, \dots, k \}.</math>

This is the closure, in the [[Zariski topology]], of the '''Schubert cell'''<ref name="KL"/><ref name="Fu"/> 
::<math>X_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathcal{V}) := \{ w \in \mathbf{Gr}(k,V)(F) : \dim (V_j \cap w) = i \text{ for all } n-k-a_i +i \leq j \leq n-k-a_{i+1} +i, \quad 1\le j \le n \} \subset \Sigma_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathcal{V}), </math>
which is used when considering [[cellular homology]] instead of the Chow ring. The latter are disjoint affine spaces, of dimension <math>|\mathbf{a}|</math>, whose union is <math> \mathbf{Gr}(k,V)</math>.

An equivalent characterization of the Schubert cell <math>X_\mathbf{a}(\mathcal{V})</math> may be given in terms of the [[flag manifold | dual complete flag]]

:<math> \tilde{\mathcal{V}}= (\tilde{V}_1 \subset \tilde{V}_2  \cdots \subset \tilde{V}_n = V),</math>

where 
:<math> \tilde{V}_i := V_n\backslash V_{n-i}, \quad i=1, \dots, n \quad (V_0:= \emptyset). </math> 

Then <math>X_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathcal{V}) \subset \mathbf{Gr}(k,V) </math> consists of those <math>k</math>-dimensional subspaces <math>w \subset V</math> that have a basis <math>(\tilde{W}_1, \dots, \tilde{W}_k)</math>
consisting of elements
:: <math>\tilde{W}_i \in \tilde{V}_{k+a_i -i +1 }, \quad i=1, \dots, k </math>

of the subspaces <math>\{\tilde{V}_{k+a_i -i +1}\}_{i=1, \dots, k}. </math>

Since the homology class <math>[\Sigma_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathcal{V})] \in A^*(\mathbf{Gr}(k,V))</math>, called a '''Schubert class''', does not depend on the choice of complete flag <math>\mathcal{V}</math>, it can be written as
::<math>\sigma_{\mathbf{a}} := [\Sigma_{\mathbf{a}}] \in A^*(\mathbf{Gr}(k,V)). </math>
It can be shown that these classes are linearly independent and generate the Chow ring as their [[linear span]]. The associated intersection theory is called '''Schubert calculus'''. For a given sequence <math>\mathbf{a} = (a_1,\ldots, a_j, 0, \ldots, 0)</math> with <math>a_j>0</math> the Schubert class <math>\sigma_{(a_1,\ldots, a_j,0,\ldots,0)}</math> is usually just denoted <math>\sigma_{(a_1,\ldots, a_j)}</math>. The Schubert classes given by a single integer <math>\sigma_{a_1}</math>, (i.e., a horizontal partition), are called '''special classes'''. Using the [[Giambelli formula]] below, all the Schubert classes can be generated from these special classes.


=== Other notational conventions ===
In some sources,<ref name="KL"/><ref name="Fu"/> the Schubert cells <math>X_\mathbf{a}</math> and Schubert varieties <math>\Sigma_\mathbf{a}</math> are labelled differently, as <math>S_\lambda </math> and <math>\bar{S}_\lambda</math>, respectively,  where <math>\lambda</math> is the ''complementary partition'' to <math>\mathbf{a}</math> with parts
::<math> \lambda_i := n-k-a_{k-i+1} </math>,
whose Young diagram is the complement of the one for <math>\mathbf{a}</math> within the <math>k \times (n-k)</math> rectangular one (reversed, both horizontally and vertically).

Another labelling convention for <math>X_\mathbf{a}</math> and <math>\Sigma_\mathbf{a}</math> is <math>C_L</math> and  
<math>\bar{C}_L</math>, respectively, where
<math>L= (L_1, \dots, L_k) \subset (1, \dots, n)</math>
is the multi-index defined by 
:: <math> L_i := n-k - a_i +i=\lambda_{k-i+1} +i. </math>

The integers <math>(L_1, \dots, L_k)</math> are the '''pivot''' locations of the representations of elements of <math>X_{\mathbf{a}}</math> in reduced matricial [[echelon form]].

=== Explanation ===
In order to explain the definition, consider a generic <math>k</math>-plane <math>w \subset V</math>. It will have only a zero intersection with <math>V_j</math> for <math>j \leq n-k</math>, whereas
:: <math>\dim(V_{j} \cap w) = i</math> for <math>j = n-k +i \geq n-k. </math> 
For example, in <math>\mathbf{Gr}(4,9)</math>, a <math>4</math>-plane <math>w</math> is the solution space of a system of five independent homogeneous linear equations. These equations will generically span when restricted to a subspace <math>V_j</math> with <math> j=\dim V_j \leq 5=9-4</math>, in which case the solution space (the intersection of  <math>V_j</math> with  <math>w</math>) will consist only of the zero vector. However, if <math>\dim(V_j) + \dim(w) > n=9</math>, <math>V_j</math> and <math>w</math> will necessarily have nonzero intersection. For example, the expected dimension of intersection of <math>V_6</math> and <math>w</math> is <math>1</math>, the intersection of <math>V_7</math> and <math>w</math> has expected dimension <math>2</math>, and so on.

The definition of a Schubert variety states that the first value of <math>j</math> with <math>\dim(V_{j} \cap w) \geq  i</math> is generically smaller than the expected value <math>n-k +i </math> by the parameter <math> a_i </math>. The <math>k</math>-planes <math>w \subset V</math> given by these constraints then define special subvarieties of <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k,n)</math>.<ref name=":0"></ref>

=== Properties ===

==== Inclusion ====
There is a partial ordering on all <math>k</math>-tuples where <math>\mathbf{a} \geq \mathbf{b}</math> if <math>a_i \geq b_i</math> for every <math>i</math>. This gives the inclusion of Schubert varieties
:: <math>\Sigma_{\mathbf{a}} \subset \Sigma_{\mathbf{b}} \iff \mathbf{a} \geq \mathbf{b},</math>

showing an increase of the indices corresponds to an even greater specialization of subvarieties.

==== Dimension formula ====
A Schubert variety <math>\Sigma_{\mathbf{a}}</math> has codimension equal to the weight 
::<math>\mathopen|\mathbf{a}\mathclose|=\sum a_i</math> 

of the partition <math>\mathbf{a}</math>.
Alternatively, in the notational convention <math>S_\lambda</math> indicated above, its dimension in <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k,n)</math> is the weight 
:: <math>\mathopen|\lambda\mathclose|= \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i = k(n-k)-\mathopen|\mathbf{a}\mathclose|.</math>   

of the complementary partition <math>\lambda \subset (n-k)^k</math> in the <math> k \times (n-k)</math> dimensional rectangular Young diagram.

This is stable under inclusions of Grassmannians. 
That is, the inclusion 
:: <math> i_{(k, n)}:\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathbf{C}^n)  \hookrightarrow \mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathbf{C}^{n+1}), \quad \mathbf{C}^n =\text{span}\{e_1, \dots, e_n\} </math>
defined, for <math>w\in\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathbf{C}^n) </math>, by
::<math>i_{(k, n)}: w \subset \mathbf{C}^n \mapsto w  \subset \mathbf{C}^n\oplus \mathbf {C} e_{n+1}  =\mathbf{C}^{n+1}
</math> 
has the property 
::<math>i^*_{(k, n)}(\sigma_{\mathbf{a}}) = \sigma_{\mathbf{a}},</math>
and the inclusion
:: <math>\tilde{i}_{(k,n)}: \mathbf{Gr}(k,n) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{Gr}(k+1,n+1)</math>
defined by adding the extra basis element <math>e_{n+1}</math> to each <math>k</math>-plane, giving a <math>(k+1)</math>-plane, 
::<math>\tilde{i}_{(k, n)}: w \mapsto w \oplus\mathbf {C} e_{n+1}   \subset \mathbf{C}^n \oplus \mathbf {C} e_{n+1}   =\mathbf{C}^{n+1}
</math> 

does as well
::<math>\tilde{i}_{(k,n)}^*(\sigma_{\mathbf{a}}) = \sigma_{\mathbf{a}}.</math>

Thus, if <math>X_{\mathbf{a}} \subset \mathbf{Gr}_k(n)</math> and <math>\Sigma_{\mathbf{a}} \subset \mathbf{Gr}_k(n)</math> are a cell and a subvariety in the Grassmannian <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(n)</math>, they may also be viewed as a cell <math>X_{\mathbf{a}} \subset \mathbf{Gr}_\tilde{k}(\tilde{n})</math> and a subvariety <math>\Sigma_{\mathbf{a}} \subset \mathbf{Gr}_\tilde{k}(\tilde{n})</math> within the Grassmannian <math>\mathbf{Gr}_\tilde{k}(\tilde{n})</math> for
any pair <math>(\tilde{k}, \tilde{n})</math> with <math> \tilde{k} \geq k</math> and 
<math> \tilde{n}-\tilde{k}  \geq n-k</math>.

=== Intersection product ===
The intersection product was first established using the '''[[Mario Pieri | Pieri]]''' and '''[[Giovanni Giambelli | Giambelli]]''' formulas.

==== Pieri formula ====
In the special case <math>\mathbf{b} = (b,0,\ldots, 0)</math>, there is an explicit formula of the product of <math>\sigma_b</math> with an arbitrary Schubert class <math>\sigma_{a_1,\ldots, a_k}</math> given by
::<math>\sigma_b\cdot\sigma_{a_1,\ldots, a_k} = \sum_{
\begin{matrix}\mathopen|c\mathclose| = \mathopen|a\mathclose| + b \\
a_i \leq c_i \leq a_{i-1}
\end{matrix} } \sigma_{\mathbf{c}},</math>

where <math>\mathopen|\mathbf{a}\mathclose| = a_1 + \cdots + a_k</math>, <math>|\mathbf{c}| = c_1 + \cdots + c_k</math> are the weights of the partitions. This  is called the '''[[Pieri formula]]''', and can be used to determine the intersection product of any two Schubert classes when combined with the '''[[Giambelli formula]]'''. For example,
::<math>\sigma_1 \cdot \sigma_{4,2,1} = \sigma_{5,2,1} + \sigma_{4,3,1} + \sigma_{4,2,1,1}. </math>

and
::<math>\sigma_2 \cdot \sigma_{4,3} = \sigma_{4,3,2} + \sigma_{4,4,1} + \sigma_{5,3,1} + \sigma_{5,4} + \sigma_{6,3} </math>

==== Giambelli formula ====
Schubert classes <math>\sigma_{\mathbf{a}}</math> for partitions of any length <math>\ell(\mathbf{a})\leq k</math> can be expressed as the determinant of a <math>(k \times k)</math> matrix having the special classes as entries. 
:: <math>\sigma_{(a_1,\ldots, a_k)} = \begin{vmatrix}
\sigma_{a_1} & \sigma_{a_1 + 1} & \sigma_{a_1 + 2} & \cdots & \sigma_{a_1 + k - 1} \\
\sigma_{a_2 - 1} & \sigma_{a_2} & \sigma_{a_2 + 1} & \cdots & \sigma_{a_2 + k - 2} \\
\sigma_{a_3 - 2} & \sigma_{a_3 - 1} & \sigma_{a_3} & \cdots & \sigma_{a_3 + k - 3} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\sigma_{a_k - k + 1} & \sigma_{a_k - k + 2} & \sigma_{a_k - k + 3} & \cdots & \sigma_{a_k}
\end{vmatrix}</math>

This is known as the '''[[Giambelli formula]]'''. It has the same form as the first [[Schur polynomials#Jacobi Trudi identities|'''Jacobi-Trudi identity''']], expressing arbitrary
[[Schur polynomial|'''Schur functions''']] <math> s_{\mathbf{a}}</math> as determinants in terms of the 
[[Schur polynomials#Jacobi Trudi identities|'''complete symmetric functions''']] <math>\{h_j := s_{(j)}\}</math>.

For example,
::<math>\sigma_{2,2} = \begin{vmatrix}
\sigma_2 & \sigma_3 \\
\sigma_1 & \sigma_2
\end{vmatrix} = \sigma_2^2 - \sigma_1\cdot\sigma_3</math>

and
::<math>\sigma_{2,1,1} = \begin{vmatrix}
\sigma_2 & \sigma_3 & \sigma_4 \\
\sigma_0 & \sigma_1 & \sigma_2 \\
0 & \sigma_0 & \sigma_1
\end{vmatrix}.</math>

==== General case ====

The intersection product between any pair of Schubert classes
<math> \sigma_{\mathbf{a}}, \sigma_{\mathbf{b}}</math> is given by
::<math> \sigma_{\mathbf{a}} \sigma_{\mathbf{b}} =\sum_{\mathbf{c}}c^\mathbf{c}_{\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b}}\sigma_{\mathbf{c}}, </math>

where <math>\{c^\mathbf{c}_{\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b}}\}</math> are the [[Littlewood-Richardson rule | Littlewood-Richardson]] coefficients.<ref name="Fu2">{{cite book | last=Fulton | first= William |author-link=William Fulton (mathematician)| title= Young Tableaux. With Applications to Representation Theory and Geometry, Chapt. 5 | year=1997 | series =London Mathematical Society Student Texts | volume = 35 |publisher=Cambridge University Press | location = Cambridge, U.K.| isbn= 9780521567244 | doi=10.1017/CBO9780511626241 }} </ref> The '''Pieri formula''' is a special case of this, when <math>\mathbf{b}=(b,0, \dots, 0)</math> has length <math>\ell(\mathbf{b})=1</math>.

== Relation with Chern classes ==
There is an easy description of the cohomology ring, or the Chow ring, of the Grassmannian  <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k,V)</math> using the Chern classes of two natural [[Vector bundle|vector bundles]] over <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k,V)</math>. We have the [[exact sequence]] of vector bundles over <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k,V)</math>
::<math>0 \to T \to \underline{V} \to Q \to 0</math>

where <math>T</math> is the '''tautological bundle''' whose fiber, over any element <math>w \in \mathbf{Gr}(k, V) </math> is the subspace <math> w \subset V</math> itself,   <math> \, \underline{V}:= \mathbf{Gr}(k,V) \times V</math> is the trivial vector bundle of rank <math>n</math>,  with <math>V</math> as fiber and <math>Q</math> is the quotient vector bundle of rank <math>n-k</math>, with <math>V/w</math> as fiber. The Chern classes of the bundles <math>T</math> and <math>Q</math>  are
::<math>c_i(T) = (-1)^i\sigma_{(1)^i},</math>

where <math>(1)^i</math> is the partition whose Young diagram consists of a single column of length <math>i</math> and
::<math>c_i(Q) = \sigma_i.</math>

The tautological sequence then gives the presentation of the Chow ring as
::<math>A^*(\mathbf{Gr}(k,V)) = \frac{\mathbb{Z}[c_1(T), \ldots, c_k(T), c_1(Q),\ldots, c_{n-k}(Q)] }{(c(T)c(Q) - 1)}.</math>

== Gr(2,4) ==
One of the classical examples analyzed is the Grassmannian <math>\mathbf{Gr}(2,4)</math> since it parameterizes lines in <math>\mathbb{P}^3</math>. Using the Chow ring <math>A^*(\mathbf{Gr}(2,4))</math>, Schubert calculus can be used to compute the number of lines on a [[cubic surface]].<ref name=":0" />

=== Chow ring ===
The Chow ring has the presentation
::<math>A^*(\mathbf{Gr}(2,4)) = \frac{\mathbb{Z}[\sigma_1,\sigma_{1,1}, \sigma_2]}{((1 - \sigma_1 + \sigma_{1,1})(1 + \sigma_1 +  \sigma_2)-1)}</math>

and as a graded [[Abelian group]]<ref>{{Cite book|last=Katz|first=Sheldon|author1-link=Sheldon Katz | title=Enumerative Geometry and String Theory|pages=96}}</ref> it is given by
:: <math>\begin{align}
A^0(\mathbf{Gr}(2,4)) &= \mathbb{Z}\cdot 1 \\
A^2(\mathbf{Gr}(2,4)) &= \mathbb{Z}\cdot \sigma_1 \\
A^4(\mathbf{Gr}(2,4)) &= \mathbb{Z}\cdot \sigma_2 \oplus \mathbb{Z} \cdot \sigma_{1,1}\\
A^6(\mathbf{Gr}(2,4)) &= \mathbb{Z}\cdot\sigma_{2,1} \\
A^8(\mathbf{Gr}(2,4)) &= \mathbb{Z}\cdot\sigma_{2,2} \\
\end{align}</math>

=== Lines on a cubic surface ===
Recall that a line in <math>\mathbb{P}^3</math> gives a dimension <math>2</math> subspace of <math>\mathbb{A}^4</math>, hence an element of <math>\mathbb{G}(1,3) \cong \mathbf{Gr}(2,4)</math>. Also, the equation of a line can be given as a section of <math>\Gamma(\mathbb{G}(1,3), T^*)</math>. Since a cubic surface <math>X</math> is given as a generic homogeneous cubic polynomial, this is given as a generic section <math>s \in \Gamma(\mathbb{G}(1,3),\text{Sym}^3(T^*))</math>. A line <math>L \subset \mathbb{P}^3</math> is a subvariety of <math>X</math> [[if and only if]] the section vanishes on <math>[L] \in \mathbb{G}(1,3)</math>. Therefore, the [[Euler class]] of <math>\text{Sym}^3(T^*)</math> can be integrated over <math>\mathbb{G}(1,3)</math> to get the number of points where the generic section vanishes on <math>\mathbb{G}(1,3)</math>. In order to get the Euler class, the total Chern class of <math>T^*</math> must be computed, which is given as
::<math>c(T^*) = 1 + \sigma_1 + \sigma_{1,1}</math>

The splitting formula then reads as the formal equation
::<math>\begin{align}
c(T^*) &= (1 + \alpha)(1 + \beta) \\
&= 1 + \alpha + \beta + \alpha\cdot\beta
\end{align},</math>

where <math>c(\mathcal{L}) = 1+\alpha</math> and <math>c(\mathcal{M}) = 1 + \beta</math> for formal line bundles <math>\mathcal{L},\mathcal{M}</math>. The splitting equation gives the relations
::<math>\sigma_1 = \alpha + \beta</math> and <math>\sigma_{1,1} = \alpha\cdot\beta</math>.

Since <math>\text{Sym}^3(T^*)</math> can be viewed as the direct sum of formal line bundles
::<math>\text{Sym}^{3}(T^{*}) = \mathcal{L}^{\otimes 3} \oplus (\mathcal{L}^{\otimes 2} \otimes \mathcal{M})
\oplus(\mathcal{L}\otimes\mathcal{M}^{\otimes 2})\oplus \mathcal{M}^{\otimes 3}</math>

whose total Chern class is
::<math>c(\text{Sym}^3(T^*)) = (1 + 3\alpha)(1 + 2\alpha + \beta)(1 + \alpha  + 2\beta)(1 + 3\beta),</math>

it follows that
::<math>\begin{align}
c_4(\text{Sym}^3(T^*)) &= 3\alpha (2\alpha + \beta) (\alpha + 2\beta) 3\beta \\
&=9\alpha\beta(2(\alpha + \beta)^2 + \alpha\beta) \\
&= 9\sigma_{1,1}(2\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_{1,1}) \\
&= 27\sigma_{2,2}\, ,
\end{align}</math>

using the fact that
::<math>\sigma_{1,1}\cdot \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_{2,1}\sigma_1 = \sigma_{2,2}</math> and <math>\sigma_{1,1}\cdot \sigma_{1,1} = \sigma_{2,2}.</math>

Since <math>\sigma_{2,2}</math> is the top class, the integral is then
::<math>\int_{\mathbb{G}(1,3)}27\sigma_{2,2} = 27.</math>

Therefore, there are <math>27</math> lines on a cubic surface.
